newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's Democrats likely to rebuff coalition offer.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Democrats likely to rebuff coalition offer.

text.p: Japan's new Democratic Party is likely to decline any offer to join in a ruling coalition led by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's conservative Liberal Democrats, a party leader said on Wednesday.
"Now is the time for us to hunker down," Yukio Hatoyama, co-leader of the Democratic Party, told Reuters in an interview.

Hatoyama said no final decision had been made, as the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) had not yet made a formal request, but added: "Basically I believe that our stance should be to start off as an opposition party."

The LDP won 239 seats in Sunday's general election, 12 short of the 251 needed for a majority in the 500-seat Lower House. It has therefore been courting its old partners in the outgoing coalition, the Social Democrats and the tiny Sakigake Party, and eyeing an alliance with the Democrats.
Sakigake has just two seats, the Social Democrats 15 and the Democrats 52. The Democratic Party was formed on September 28 by defectors from the Social Democrats and Sakigake.

Hatoyama, a former Sakigake leader and a one-time member of a reformist coalition that ended the LDP's monopoly on power in 1993, said the Democrats feared losing their influence if they joined a ruling bloc led by the LDP when its own numbers were as yet relatively small.

But with more than 50 seats, the Democrats -- ardent advocates of trimming government and reducing bureaucrats' grip on policy -- would still have the ability to introduce their own bills in parliament as an opposition party, he added.
Hatoyama also questioned the LDP's commitment to real administrative reform, despite the fact that Hashimoto made calls for such changes a centrepiece of his campaign.

He reiterated his party's support for a planned rise in the consumption tax to five percent from three percent next April, and said some sort of extra budget for the current fiscal year to next March 31 would be needed.

But he cast doubt on the advisability of crafting a five trillion yen ($44.6 billion) budget including three trillion yen ($26.7 billion) worth of public works spending, as advocated by some senior LDP members during the campaign.
